title: Erin Patterson: Mushroom murderer launches last-ditch High Court appeal
description: Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.Erin Patterson, 5
body: Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.Erin Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday. She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

schema.headline: Erin Patterson: Mushroom murderer launches last-ditch High Court appeal

title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
description: Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.The pair were technicians working
body: Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war. The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.Italy's foreign minister was quoted by Italian media as saying that investigations showed that the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran and that Iranian proxies were known to carry out attacks in the region."The Rheinmetall Group is in deep mourning," the German firm said in a statement confirming the deaths of two of its staff members."Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, as they were providing technical support for air defence systems," it added."Protecting people in the country was a matter of profound importance to them."Company management and the workforce are devastated that our colleagues have now lost their lives."Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.The men had been performing maintenance on systems used by the Kuwait Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa citing Italy's foreign ministry.Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families. "My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf."Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

schema.headline: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility

title: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
description: An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.Eyewitnesses share
body: An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery. On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges. It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

schema.headline: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion

title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
description: Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before hi
body: Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation. The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime."In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland.""I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged issue in Italy.The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she had been "deeply shocked" by the case. "His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.The letter was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres". Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death

title: Grace Tame: Ex-media executive admits saying child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
description: Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she h
body: Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit."My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey."The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste"."I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink"."But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm"."It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011."They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks."I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry."I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

schema.headline: Grace Tame: Ex-media executive admits saying child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'

title: Marital rape: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected - study
description: South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Sa
body: South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriageMarital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdictIndia government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan. A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it."The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC."But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal." The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region. In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh". India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on itIndia anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then diedRights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says."Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says. "They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year. In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

schema.headline: Marital rape: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected - study

title: Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
description: Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.The public p
body: Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act"."He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.

schema.headline: Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31

title: Rebecca Taylor: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
description: A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a pr
body: A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning. The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update. The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said."It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying. All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed. The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

schema.headline: Rebecca Taylor: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment

title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling
description: Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has
body: Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report."Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick. While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders.Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

schema.headline: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling

title: Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
description: Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.Eastern ar
body: Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us. Conditions are forecast now to improve, though the National Weather Service (NWS) cautions that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms. Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk. On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.The number of homes reporting power cuts peaked at close to a million on Thursday evening - with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey badly affected. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. In Maryland, almost two million customers were asked by authorities to limit their water consumption to essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".Parts of eastern states are under states of emergency, including New York. Organisers of New York City's annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have also postponed the iconic event to Saturday.

schema.headline: Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving

title: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
description: Figure caption, Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's musicByMusic correspondentUpdated 26 November 2026Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod
body: Figure caption, Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's musicByMusic correspondentUpdated 26 November 2026Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music."His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart"."Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."Figure caption, Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order,  recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You. Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songsThe son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and new wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980sDuran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs. Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.They became so popular in the US that the press labeled them the leaders of a "second British invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station. The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid."We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy. "We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."He went on to play on Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.Image source, PAImage caption, Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse MacabreAfter a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again. In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion. When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.The following BBC programmes will pay tribute to Taylor: Duran Duran at the BBC, on BBC Four on Friday 27 November at 21:30 GMTSounds of the 80s, on Radio 2 on Saturday 28 November at at 18:00 GMT

schema.headline: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65

title: EU leaders fail to bridge budget splits as talks stall
description: European Union (EU) leaders have deferred negotiations on its long-term budget after tensions surfaced over the bloc's spending priorities and aid for
body: European Union (EU) leaders have deferred negotiations on its long-term budget after tensions surfaced over the bloc's spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.Tense talks on the 2028-34 budget ended after 12 hours on Thursday at a summit in Brussels, with some members walking out of negotiations that will resume in December.Divisions were largely split along the lines of countries, including France and Italy, wanting to approve a higher-spending proposal against those advocating for financial restraint, with Germany chief among them.Many members want the budget locked in ahead of several high-stakes elections held across Europe in 2027, including in France.Countries remain divided over a proposal to provide Ukraine with an additional loan of €45bn (£37.6bn), split between non-military and military funding.Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary have objected to the loan, but German Chancellor Frederich Merz said uniform EU agreement was a condition for approving the broader budget."I stand by my view that aid for Ukraine must be supported by the European Union as a whole," Merz told reporters."The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."Bulgaria, which previously opposed the plan, said it would agree to fund part of the loan that commits non-military financial support to Kyiv, marking a small sign of progress emerging from the special summit of the European Council. EU members have been wrangling over the long-term budget after the European Commission submitted a €2tn proposal earlier this year, with some countries objecting to high levels of spending. Those advocating higher spending want the funds to future-proof industries such as farming and invest in regional development. Fiscally cautious countries want to avoid amassing ballooning debt.Thursday's talks were set up by the European Council to unblock the impasse, with a proposal to reduce spending by approximately €220bn to €230bn.Under the current proposal, the budget totals €1.582tn, which includes €140bn to repay pandemic-era borrowing.Four countries wanting to rein in the budget, including Denmark and Austria, walked out of negotiations after several hours of meetings.Merz said there was "new movement" towards reducing the size of the EU budget, though he added "we are not there yet" when he confirmed that a new round of negotiations would not take place in Brussels on Friday.European budgets requires approval from all 27 countries, with each country effectively holding veto power. French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to lower long-term spending.France's forthcoming presidential election came into focus during the EU budget  talks, with frontrunner Marine Le Pen calling the talks an "underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people".Last month, Le Pen announced she would significantly reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if she were to win the presidency. Macron addressed Le Pen's remarks on the sidelines of the Brussels summit, saying: "It is an odd kind of arrogance to behave as if she is already in charge of France's destiny because, as things stand, she has not been elected." Once the talks concluded, the European Council announced a two-day summit on 17 and 18 December would revive budget negotiations.Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos was also named as the next President of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde from February 2027.

schema.headline: EU leaders fail to bridge budget splits as talks stall

title: Noida: 164 foreigners rescued from cyberfraud racket
description: Police in India say they have uncovered an international cyberfraud and human trafficking operation on the outskirts of capital city Delhi and rescued
body: Police in India say they have uncovered an international cyberfraud and human trafficking operation on the outskirts of capital city Delhi and rescued 92 Indonesian and 72 Malaysian nationals.They were allegedly lured to India with promises of lucrative IT jobs, but forced into cyber crime, according to police.Police say the scheme was exposed after a Malaysian worker managed to escape and revealed the operation.Dozens of foreign nationals have alleged that once they arrived in India, their passports were confiscated and they were held against their will in Noida - a Delhi suburb that is a major IT and business hub in northern India and home to several call centres.Instead of the jobs and high salaries promised, police say, they were forced to pose as women online to lure unsuspecting victims into fake investment platforms.So far one Malaysian national has been arrested in connection with the crime, and nearly 550 desktop computers, laptops and mobile phones have been confiscated, police say.An investigation has now been launched into a potential wider global cyberfraud network.Police and Indian banks have been trying to contend with an alarming rise in cyber fraud operations in recent years.A paper, external by the Reserve Bank of India warned against rising digital fraud and "the manipulation of users through social engineering, coercion, or impersonation".Figures from India's National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal show 2.8 million cyber fraud complaints were recorded in 2025, with losses of about 22,495 crore rupees, external ($2.42bn; £1.85 bn). It's a dramatic rise in complaints by more than 4,000% since 2021.The federal government said most cases involved fake investment and trading scams. In fake investment scams, fraudsters approach victims through social media, messaging groups or phone calls, posing as financial experts and promising high returns.They lure victims to fake trading platforms that show fictitious profits. Some are allowed to withdraw small amounts to build trust, but when they try to cash out larger sums, they are blocked or asked to pay more. The fraudsters eventually disappear with their money.The Noida case is the latest in a series of international cyberfraud call centres busted in north India in recent months, with police raids in Lucknow and Delhi's Pitampura area.In July, Lucknow Police arrested 119 people after raiding a fake international call centre targeting US citizens. Employees allegedly posed as representatives of major companies and US government agencies to defraud victims.Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external Twitter, external and Facebook, external.

title: Med Emre: Diesel tanker carrying tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
description: An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.The Med E
body: An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service."There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X. Elena Delgado, maritime captain of Valencia, told news agency AFP that a small slick that had formed around the boat had "disappeared". "The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out on Friday morning. Earlier, regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had originally been reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
description: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in deliv
body: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin."Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English."He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.He said talks were expected to resume in December.On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.The Kremlin appears to be resisting.Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect"."When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin."You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems."It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said."The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.So whose decision was that?"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.He declined to be more specific.But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.They have also plunged much of the city into darkness."[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said."People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."
